rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2 Method - semi-structured interviews with 82 farmers and managers of 5 WUAs in three irrigation systems in 2011-2012, plus WUA internal documents and field observations. Q2: Section 4.2 Changes in operating rules - new rules implemented to distribute water among farmers after drip: Vall d'Uixo WUA sets a maximum daily water use with automatic valve closure; a JTC WUA sets a volume limit above which price is higher; the ARJ sets a flow-rate limit per plot with technical guidelines checked before admission; Section 3.3 - some WUAs made drip connection compulsory or priced gravity higher; Section 5.1 - WUAs merged (19 to 12 in Vall d'Uixo), share ceding in JTC, centralization of sector management in the ARJ Governing Board. Q5: Section 2 and Table 1 - three distinct irrigation districts (JTC, ARJ, Vall d'Uixo) with different water sources and organizations, and rule changes reported separately for each in Sections 4.2 and 5.1. Q6: Table 1 and Sections 4.2, 5.1 - rules and institutional changes reported at WUA/district scale (2,395 to 19,437 ha). Q7: Section 4.1 and Section 6 - authors state that where a high level of automation and remote control exists, decisions are the responsibility of the WUA and it is easier to concentrate decision-making centrally, whereas in non-automatic systems farmers keep scheduling decisions; Section 3.3 - a high share of unconnected farmers would create serious management problems, motivating compulsory connection rules.
rows.notes: Q3 no: findings rest on interviews (farmers and managers are the same method); internal documents and field observations are mentioned in Method but no result on new rules is attributed to them independently. Q4 no: automation is described qualitatively as the pathway to centralized rules but not measured or modelled. Q5 yes is given with some doubt: the three districts share the same region, climate and dominant citrus crop, but are institutionally distinct schemes with results reported for each. Q8: no explicit limitations of the interview-based findings stated. Q9: only percentages, no dispersion measures.

rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2 Method - own interview data from 82 farmers (70 with drip) and 5 WUA managements. Q2: Section 3.2 Farmer's perspectives - first reason for adopting drip was WUA obligation (50%), then increased production (16%); only 9% mentioned water saving; other drivers were product quality, convenience, labour savings; Section 4.2 - a technician practices 'psychological irrigation' (irrigating above crop needs), managers report farmers in some transformed sectors use the same water as before drip and are given additional water on demand; Section 6 - water saving goals become blurred down the top-down chain and water saving potential vanishes when these operating procedures are applied. Q6: Sections 4.2, 4.3 and 6 - reported at WUA/sector/district scale across three schemes (managers' statements about transformed sectors; ARJ reinstating gravity irrigation in various sectors). Q7: Sections 4.2 and 6 - authors state the water saving potential vanishes when WUAs supply water beyond crop requirements, gravity networks are kept to complement drip and farmers add fertilizer; managers state they will have to pressure farmers to reduce demand in order to realize the water saving potential, i.e. WUA enforcement of volumes is stated as a condition for conservation.
rows.notes: Q3 no: all evidence on motivations and water use comes from interviews (farmers, managers, technician); no measured water-use data of the authors' own (basin-level withdrawal figures are cited from Sanchis-Ibor et al. 2017). Q4 no: the intermediate variable (water actually applied under drip) is not measured; practices such as over-irrigation and dual drip/furrow use are only reported qualitatively from interviews. Q5 no: motivation percentages are pooled across the 82 farmers, not reported per district. Q8: no limitations stated for the interview findings. Q9: no dispersion measures. The basin-scale part of the passage (efficiency gains not translating to basin conservation) is discussed rather than demonstrated by the study's own data.

notes: Full text available including references. Qualitative socio-institutional case study based on semi-structured interviews in three Valencian collective irrigation systems; no quantitative water-use measurements, no uncertainty measures and no explicit limitations section.
